tweet_summary: A donation-soliciting account posts a dramatic claim (256k impressions) that Ukrainian forces broke through the front in late March 2026, that Russian defenses 'collapsed' and enemy positions surrendered en masse, accompanied by a generic photo of advancing Ukrainian troops/armor.
why_note_decision: A note is warranted. The claim of a sudden Russian collapse and mass surrender of positions in late March 2026 is contradicted by the Institute for the Study of War: that period saw only incremental gains and grinding, contested front lines, with Russia still slowly advancing (ISW: ~17 sq mi gained by Russia the week of Mar 24-31). There was no breakthrough, no collapse, no liberation of cities. The accompanying image carries an 'SC9' watermark suggesting it is generic/recycled footage, not documentation of the claimed event. Readers benefit from the factual context.
judge_guidance: PASS only if the note establishes that, as of late March 2026, there was NO Ukrainian breakthrough, NO collapse of Russian defenses, and NO mass surrender / liberation of cities — credible assessments (ISW) describe only incremental gains and stalled, contested front lines, with Russia still making slow advances. The note MUST cite a loadable, authoritative source for the front-line status (e.g. ISW / criticalthreats.org assessment for late March 2026, or AP/Reuters/Al Jazeera war coverage). FAIL the original note's specific failure: ensure the cited URLs actually load and substantiate the 'no breakthrough' claim (the original was rated notHelpfulSourcesMissingOrUnreliable). Optionally the note may note the image appears to be generic/unrelated footage, but only if it does not over-claim about media it cannot verify. FAIL any note that endorses the breakthrough/collapse narrative.
reference_note: As of late March 2026 there was no Ukrainian breakthrough or collapse of Russian defenses. The Institute for the Study of War describes grinding, contested front lines with only incremental gains on both sides; Russia continued to make slow advances and no cities were liberated in a sudden offensive. https://www.criticalthreats.org/analysis/russian-offensive-campaign-assessment-march-31-2026 https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/3/28/russian-strikes-on-ukraine-cities-kill-4-as-deal-to-end-war-dims
original_note_text: There are no credible reports of a major Ukrainian breakthrough, collapse of Russian defenses, or the liberation of cities as of late March 2026. Experts describe only incremental gains in the south and stalled front lines.     https://understandingwar.org/research/russia-ukraine/russian-offensive-campaign-assessment-march-26-2026   https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/3/28/russian-strikes-on-ukraine-cities-kill-4-as-deal-to-end-war-dims
failure_reason: Rated notHelpfulSourcesMissingOrUnreliable (5) on a low-volume (12) note. The verdict is correct and well-aligned with ISW, but the lead ISW URL uses an 'understandingwar.org/research/...' path that may not resolve cleanly (ISW assessments are commonly hosted at criticalthreats.org), and the small rating pool flagged sourcing. Substantively sound but the citation reliability is the weak point.
importance_lens_rationale: Wartime morale/disinformation (256k impressions) overstating battlefield success; inflated 'collapse' narratives distort public understanding of the war and peace-deal prospects. Moderate public-interest value.

tweet_summary: A 1.7M-follower account posts a meme with two attributed quotes — a Reagan quote ('If fascism ever comes to America, it will come in the name of liberalism') and a Churchill quote ('The fascists of the future will call themselves anti-fascists') — captioned 'We're watching it happen.'
why_note_decision: The Churchill quote is a well-documented fabrication he never said ('Churchillian Drift'), and the Reagan quote is at best unverifiable / commonly misattributed (a variant of a Sinclair Lewis-style maxim). Presenting fabricated quotes from revered historical figures as authentic political authority to 1.7M followers warrants a note, contrary to the provisional no-note.
judge_guidance: PASS only if the note establishes that the Churchill quote is fabricated (Churchill never said it). A strong note ALSO flags that the Reagan attribution is unverified/commonly misattributed. It must AVOID the original note's failure of addressing only one quote: the original note debunked just the Churchill line and ignored the equally prominent Reagan line, so a note that names BOTH is the bar. Must cite a credible source for the Churchill debunk (Snopes / Hillsdale Churchill Project / PolitiFact). Do NOT pass a note that treats either quote as genuine.
reference_note: Neither quote is reliably authentic. Churchill never said 'the fascists of the future will call themselves anti-fascists' — it's a long-debunked misattribution (the Hillsdale Churchill Project finds no record of it). The Reagan line ('fascism...in the name of liberalism') is also unverified and widely misattributed, echoing a Sinclair Lewis-style maxim. https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/fascists-called-anti-fascists-quote/ https://winstonchurchill.hillsdale.edu/fascists-anti-fascists/ https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/ronald-reagan-fascism-liberalism/

failure_reason: Correct but incomplete: the meme features TWO attributed quotes and the note only debunks the Churchill one, leaving the Reagan quote (also unverified/misattributed) unaddressed — a MissingKeyPoints failure for a two-quote image.
importance_lens_rationale: 237k impressions from a 1.7M-follower account weaponizing fake historical quotes for political framing; debunking fabricated 'authority' quotes has modest civic-epistemic value.

tweet_summary: Shadow Energy Secretary Claire Coutinho (UK Conservative MP) tweets that 'just 0.8% of those benefitting from lifting the 2 child benefit cap are children of British workers' and that '99% of those families are either not in work or not British', citing DWP analysis.
why_note_decision: Misleading numerical framing. The 0.8% figure (3,700 of 470,000 households) refers specifically to households where BOTH parents are British-born AND work full-time — the narrow group covered by Reform's conditional proposal. Coutinho generalizes this to '99% are not in work or not British', which obscures that the 99.2% remainder includes many British single-parent working households, British two-parent households where only one works full-time, etc. Labour Press, GBNews, and other sources confirm the original figure is specifically about two-parent full-time-working British-born households. A note clarifying what the 0.8% actually measures is warranted.
judge_guidance: PASS if the note explains that the 0.8% figure refers specifically to households where BOTH parents are British-born and work full-time (per Reform's conditional pledge), NOT all working British families — so the tweet's framing that '99% are not in work or not British' is misleading because it excludes single-parent working families, part-time working families, and mixed-status households. Bonus credit for citing the actual DWP / Labour analysis numbers (3,700 out of 470,000). FAIL if the note (a) accepts the tweet's framing, (b) just argues policy without addressing the statistical misrepresentation, or (c) cites only partisan sources.
reference_note: The 0.8% figure (3,700 of 470,000 households) is from DWP analysis of Reform's specific proposal to lift the cap only for households where BOTH parents are British-born AND work full-time. Most of the other 99.2% include single-parent working families and partially-employed British households — not, as the tweet implies, families who are uniformly 'not in work or not British'. https://www.gbnews.com/politics/labour-two-child-benefits-cap-reform-uk
original_note_text: The 0.8% figure from the cited DWP/Labour analysis refers to households with two full-time working British-born parents (per Reform's proposal), not all children of British workers, as over half of affected households have at least one worker. https://www.theguardian.com/politics/2026/jan/07/racchel-reeves-nigel-farage-two-child-benefit-cap-comments https://www.independent.co.uk/news/uk/politics/farage-pledge-child-benefit-cap-poverty-b2889710.html https://www.thecanary.co/uk/analysis/2025/07/30/dwp-two-child-limit-news/
failure_reason: Note is substantively correct but rated 13x 'missing key points' and 13x 'note not needed'. The text is dense and slightly hard to parse — the key point (0.8% = both-parents-full-time-British-born, not all working British families) could be stated more crisply. Also, citing thecanary.co (a partisan left outlet) likely hurts perceived neutrality.
importance_lens_rationale: UK policy debate about ~470k children in poverty + immigration framing reaching 420k impressions; statistical misrepresentation by a sitting Shadow Cabinet minister is high-value to correct.

tweet_summary: Tweet (16M impressions) shows a Dutch judge handing a 'migrant killer of a little girl just 120 hours community service'; the father throws a chair. Tweet posted Dec 2025, framing it as current.
why_note_decision: The clip is from a 2014 Roermond court ruling on a 2013 Meijel crash where a 35-year-old Polish national, speeding, killed a 2-year-old girl and her grandparents on a cycle path. Prosecutors appealed; in September 2015 an appeals court sentenced him to 15 months in jail (plus a 4-year driving ban); he was later extradited from the UK and served the sentence. Sharing the 2014 outburst in Dec 2025 without that context misleadingly implies the lenient sentence stood. The tweet also misframes a Polish EU-citizen driver as 'migrant killer' in a clearly anti-immigration register. A note IS warranted. The original note correctly supplies the appeal + 15-month outcome but doesn't address the 'migrant' framing (the driver was a Polish national) or that the clip is over a decade old.
judge_guidance: PASS if the note (1) flags the clip is from 2014 (not current), AND (2) states the appeals court overturned the 120-hour sentence in September 2015 and imposed 15 months in jail, which the driver served after extradition. Bonus: note that the driver was a Polish (EU) national. FAIL notes that (a) treat the 120 hours as the final sentence, (b) endorse the 'migrant killer' framing, or (c) just say the tweet is fake without explaining the appeal/extradition. The original note is close — it covers (1) and (2), so a similar quality note should pass.
reference_note: This is a 2014 ruling on a 2013 Meijel crash where a Polish (EU national) driver killed a 2-year-old and her grandparents on a cycle path. Prosecutors appealed: a Sept 2015 appeals court overturned the 120-hour sentence and imposed 15 months in jail plus a 4-year driving ban. He was extradited from the UK and served the sentence. https://www.dutchnews.nl/2015/09/appeal-court-jails-driver-for-killing-couple-and-grandchild/ https://nltimes.nl/2016/08/24/polish-fugitive-extradited-netherlands-serve-sentence-fatal-accident
original_note_text: Misleading: the clip shows a 2014 outburst after an initial 120-hour community service sentence, but prosecutors appealed and an appeals court later sentenced the driver to 15 months' jail; he was extradited to serve that term. https://www.dutchnews.nl/2015/09/appeal-court-jails-driver-for-killing-couple-and-grandchild/
failure_reason: missing_key_points: covers the appeal correctly but doesn't address the 'migrant killer' framing (the driver was a Polish EU national), nor that the original tweet uses a 11+ year old clip to imply a current ruling
importance_lens_rationale: 16M impressions weaponizing an 11-year-old clip in an anti-immigration register; correcting the temporal/appeal context matters for honest democratic discourse.

tweet_summary: A pro-Trump account posts an animated 'LayoffHedge' infographic captioned 'Graph shows H-1B visa holders legally migrating to the United States,' showing cumulative figures rising to ~6.9M by 2025, implying that many H-1B workers are entering the US.
why_note_decision: The animation's own labels say it tracks cumulative LCA (Labor Condition Application) filings 2015-2025, NOT actual H-1B visa holders migrating. New H-1B visas are statutorily capped at 85,000/year (65,000 + 20,000 advanced-degree), and the total active H-1B population is roughly 600,000-750,000 — far below the ~6.9M figure. An LCA is a prerequisite employers file; one worker/position can generate multiple filings and many never become visas. why_note_decision: There is no CBS News poll showing Republican Trump approval at 92.5% (or 92.3%). CBS's published polls in this period (CBS News/YouGov) actually show Trump with a -26 net approval overall; CNN/SSRS at 80% Republican approval, Pew at 68%. The same fabricated 92%+ figure recycles across parody and non-parody accounts. CNN explicitly fact-checked a parallel '100% Republican approval' claim. Reaches >160K views and is presented as breaking news — a note is clearly warranted.
judge_guidance: PASS if the note (a) clearly states no such CBS poll exists / CBS has not released a poll with that figure, and (b) gives actual recent Republican-approval numbers from credible polling (e.g. CNN/SSRS ~80%, Pew ~68%, or CBS/YouGov's actual numbers). Strong notes cite CBS News polls archive plus a real outside fact-check (CNN, AP, Reuters) or Pew/Gallup/Quinnipiac numbers. FAIL if the bot just says 'CBS hasn't released this' with only Wikipedia/Rasmussen as supporting links (this is the original note's weakness — raters flagged sources as unreliable). FAIL if the bot declines (the figure is fabricated, high-confidence). FAIL if the bot accepts the 92.5% figure.

tweet_summary: Quote-tweet ('as close as we can get to a POV of being hit by a ballistic missile') amplifying a quoted video framed as an Iranian ballistic-missile strike on Prince Sultan Air Base in Al-Kharj, Saudi Arabia, hitting near US servicemembers with only minor injuries.
why_note_decision: A note is warranted: the quoted video is recycled footage sold as a current war event. Full Fact (3 Mar) and PolitiFact (4 Mar) confirm the clip is the aftermath of a July 2024 Israeli airstrike on Yemen's Hodeidah port, not a 2026 Saudi strike. A commenter explicitly says 'This is an old video and NOT in Saudi Arabia'. As of the 6 Mar tweet date, the real missiles toward Prince Sultan Air Base were intercepted by Saudi defenses with no impact on the base.
judge_guidance: PASS only if the note (a) tells the reader the video does NOT show a 2026 Iranian missile strike on Prince Sultan Air Base, and (b) identifies it as recycled/old footage (the July 2024 Israeli airstrike on Yemen's Hodeidah/Hudaydah port) OR otherwise establishes misattribution, backed by a verifiable fact-check (Full Fact / PolitiFact / AFP). The note may add that the 6 Mar 2026 missiles fired at the base were intercepted with no impact, but MUST NOT assert as flat permanent fact that no Iranian missile ever struck the base (a later strike damaged US aircraft) and MUST NOT just concede the Prince-Sultan framing. FAIL if it repeats the false premise that this clip shows the base being hit, cites sources about a different clip, or makes an absolute claim that later became incorrect.
reference_note: This is old footage, not a 2026 Iranian strike on Saudi Arabia. Fact-checkers identified it as the aftermath of a July 2024 Israeli airstrike on Yemen's Hodeidah port. Iran did fire missiles toward Prince Sultan Air Base on March 6, 2026, but Saudi defenses intercepted them with no impact on the base. https://fullfact.org/conflict/iran-bomb-us-airbase-saudi-arabia-video-false https://www.politifact.com/factchecks/2026/mar/04/tweets/iran-strikes-airbase-yemen-explosion/
original_note_text: This video shows a July 2024 Israeli airstrike on Yemen's Hudaydah port, not an Iranian missile impact at Prince Sultan Air Base. Saudi defenses intercepted the missiles; no strikes hit the base and no injuries occurred.    https://factcheck.afp.com/doc.afp.com.99J43G3 https://fullfact.org/conflict/iran-bomb-us-airbase-saudi-arabia-video-false https://www.arabnews.com/node/2635432/saudi-arabia https://www.jpost.com/middle-east/iran-news/article-889040
failure_reason: Rated notHelpfulIncorrect (6) plus notHelpfulIrrelevantSources (4). The video identification (July 2024 Yemen footage) is correct and well-sourced. The note was flagged 'incorrect' on its over-reaching second sentence — the absolute claims 'no strikes hit the base and no injuries occurred' were contested in the fog of war (a service member was reported injured/killed in 1 Mar attacks, and later strikes damaged aircraft), so the blanket no-impact/no-injury assertion overstated certainty even though the core debunk was right.
importance_lens_rationale: 1.3M impressions amplifying recycled war footage in an active Iran-Saudi-US conflict; correcting fog-of-war misattribution that fuels escalation is EA/progress-relevant.

tweet_summary: A NewsWire post states 'Israel, United States and Argentina vote against U.N. resolution to condemn slavery; UK and EU nations abstain.'
why_note_decision: A note is warranted: the framing 'vote against a resolution to condemn slavery' is materially misleading. The March 25, 2026 UN General Assembly resolution (A/80/L.48) did not merely condemn slavery; it declared the transatlantic slave trade the gravest crime against humanity AND called on member states to engage in reparatory-justice talks (apology, restitution, compensation). The US, Israel and Argentina voted no, and the EU abstained, primarily over the reparations/retroactive-international-law provisions, not because they endorse slavery. The headline collapses a vote on a specific reparations-and-ranking resolution into 'voting against condemning slavery.'
judge_guidance: PASS only if the note clarifies WHAT the resolution actually was - i.e. that it declared transatlantic slavery the gravest crime against humanity and recommended reparations/reparatory justice - and that the 'no' votes / abstentions were about those provisions (reparations, retroactive legal liability, ranking of crimes), not an endorsement of slavery. FAIL if the note accepts the 'voted against condemning slavery' framing, takes a partisan side on whether reparations are merited, or omits the reparations element that is the crux of the dispute. Neutral, factual explanation of the resolution's content is required.
reference_note: The vote was against a resolution declaring transatlantic slavery the worst crime against humanity and recommending reparations, not against slavery overall.    https://news.un.org/en/story/2026/03/1167199     https://usun.usmission.gov/explanation-of-vote-for-unga-resolution/
importance_lens_rationale: 2.2M impressions; a politically charged headline that distorts a real UN vote into 'pro-slavery,' inflaming polarization. Correcting it serves both factual accuracy and depolarization in a high-emotion topic.

tweet_summary: Claims Russia confirmed a cancer vaccine that 'will soon be offered free to patients around the world,' reshaping global cancer care; image shows Putin holding a 'CANCER VACCINE' vial with the headline 'free to patients all over the world.'
why_note_decision: The 'free to patients all over the world' claim is false/misleading. Russian officials (including Putin) said the vaccine (Enteromix) would be offered free to cancer patients in Russia upon approval (~late 2025) — there is no plan, financing, or regulatory pathway to provide it free worldwide; it has not been submitted to the FDA, EMA, or other regulators and is unavailable outside Russia. Efficacy claims are also overstated: it is in early trials targeting specific cancers, with no published proof of broad effectiveness. This is a checkable, high-reach health-misinformation claim, so a note is warranted.
judge_guidance: PASS only if the note corrects the central falsehood — the vaccine is not going to be free 'to patients all over the world'; Russia announced free availability only domestically (in Russia) upon approval. Strong notes also flag that it remains in trials (not proven, not approved internationally, targeting specific cancers like colorectal/melanoma), and is not available outside Russia. The note must NOT endorse the 'free worldwide' or 'reshape global cancer care' framing as accurate, and must NOT simply call the entire vaccine fake (the program is real but early-stage). Cite credible fact-checks/reporting (Snopes, Newsweek, AFP, Reuters). Avoid relying solely on Russian state media.
reference_note: Russian officials said this vaccine (Enteromix) would be offered free to cancer patients in Russia upon approval, not free to patients worldwide. It is still in early trials, has not been approved by international regulators (FDA/EMA), is unavailable outside Russia, and targets specific cancers rather than all types. https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/russia-enteromix-mrna-cancer-vaccine/ https://www.newsweek.com/russia-cancer-vaccine-enteromix-claims-trials-2126451
importance_lens_rationale: 576k impressions on a health-misinformation claim about a cancer 'cure'; false hope about free worldwide cancer vaccines can distort patient expectations and decisions — high value to correct from a public-health lens.

description.description:
A sequence of four frames demonstrating a safety issue with an electric water heater and its solution. 

1. The first frame is a conceptual illustration showing a person showering. Red lines indicate a dangerous electrical path from the water heater through the water pipes and splashing water onto the person.
2. The second frame shows a real-world scenario where a person uses a voltage tester pen on the metal hose of a wall-mounted water heater labeled "热水器" (Water Heater). The pen glows green, indicating live electricity is present on the plumbing.
3. The third frame shows hands disconnecting the flexible metal hose from the heater's inlet and outlet connections to prepare for the installation of safety devices.
4. The fourth frame shows the installation of two "anti-electric wall" (insulation) devices directly onto the heater ports. These devices are designed to create a high-resistance path to prevent electric shocks in the event of a heater leak.

**Khalid** (@toplevl)  
Water heaters cause electrocution not because water conducts electricity, but because of faulty electrical and grounding conditions. Here’s how it happens: 
Faulty internal wiring or heating element
Inside electric water heaters are live heating elements. If the insulation around these elements degrades or cracks, electricity can leak into the water or the metal tank.

Poor or missing earthing (grounding)
If the heater is not properly earthed, any leaked current has nowhere safe to go. Instead, the metal body, pipes, or water itself can become energized.

Water as a path, not the source
Pure water isn’t a good conductor, but household water contains minerals and salts. This makes it conductive enough to carry current to anyone touching the water or connected plumbing.

Human body completes the circuit
When a person touches the energized water or metal while also in contact with ground (wet floor, concrete, bare feet), their body becomes the shortest path to earth; resulting in electrocution.

Absence of safety devices
Without an RCD/ELCB (residual current device), even small leakages won’t trip the power. The current keeps flowing until someone gets shocked.

Damaged plumbing connections
Metal pipes can transmit electricity from a faulty heater to taps, shower heads, or bathroom fittings, even outside the bathroom.

Why bathrooms are especially dangerous
Wet skin has very low resistance. That’s why even small voltages can become fatal in bathrooms.

tweet_summary: An explainer video by a popular science/engineering account showing how faulty electric water heaters can energize plumbing and electrocute bathers, and demonstrating an 'anti-electric wall' (water-resistance insulation) device fitted to the heater's hose connections as a mitigation.
why_note_decision: The tweet is a broadly accurate safety explainer, not a misleading claim. Electric water heaters CAN cause electrocution via degraded heating-element insulation, missing grounding, and absence of RCD/ELCB protection (corroborated by the detailed top comments and by electrical-safety sources). The 'anti-electric wall' device is a real, patented Chinese product (CN201028801Y) that lengthens the water path to raise resistance and limit leakage current. Nothing checkable in the tweet is false; the only quibbles in replies are about whether the isolator alone is sufficient vs. needing grounding+RCD, which is an engineering nuance, not misinformation warranting a public correction. The note merely appends standard advice (grounding, GFCI/RCD) and contradicts nothing in the post.
judge_guidance: PASS only if the bot declines to write a note. This is a substantially accurate DIY/safety explainer about a real hazard and a real (patented) mitigation device; any note here is a false positive. A note that 'corrects' the tweet by implying the device is fake/useless, or that the electrocution mechanism is wrong, should FAIL outright. A note that merely adds supplementary safety tips (grounding/RCD) without correcting any false claim is also a fail, because no correction is warranted.
original_note_text: The anti-electric wall device, used in some countries, reduces shock risk by making the water path longer to limit current flow. Standard measures also include proper grounding and GFCI/RCD protection in wet areas. https://patents.google.com/patent/CN201028801Y/en https://www.esfi.org/understanding-your-home-electrical-system
failure_reason: Note corrects nothing — the tweet is accurate. It only appends supplementary safety info, so raters tagged it both NoteNotNeeded and MissingKeyPoints. It is a false positive: no misleading claim to correct.
importance_lens_rationale: 545K views and a real-world electrocution hazard; from a progress/safety lens, accurate DIY safety content is net-positive and should not be suppressed by a spurious note.

Account bio says 'PARODY ACCOUNT. Don't take the posts seriously,' but the post itself has no parody indicator and many replies (e.g. 'A man comfortable in his masculinity', 'huge shift from her last marriage') engage with the quote as real.
why_note_decision: A note IS warranted despite the parody label. Although the account bio identifies as parody, the individual tweet does not — and at 2.6M views with replies treating the quote as a real statement, the parody disclaimer is functionally invisible to most viewers. Fabricated quotes attributed to identifiable real people (Maxx Morando is a real musician engaged to Miley Cyrus since Dec 2 2025) are exactly the kind of unattributed misinformation Community Notes is designed to flag. The note's two corrections (fabricated quote + boyfriend vs. fiancé) are both accurate and useful. Provisional 'no_note_needed' undervalues how parody-account quote fabrications about real celebrities can spread as genuine.
judge_guidance: PASS only if the note (a) flags the quote as fabricated with no credible source, AND (b) flags that the account is a self-declared parody account (per bio), AND ideally (c) notes Morando is Cyrus's fiancé (engaged Dec 2 2025 at Avatar: Fire and Ash premiere, per Rolling Stone/People/ABC News), not 'boyfriend' Max. AVOID citing only that the engagement is recent — the core misleader is the fabricated quote. A note that ONLY corrects boyfriend→fiancé while leaving the fake quote unchallenged FAILS. A note that treats the post as a genuine statement and tries to debate the substance FAILS. Source should be a credible outlet (Rolling Stone, People, ABC News, Yahoo).

Don't take the posts seriously.'). Morando is also Cyrus's fiancé, not 'boyfriend' — they got engaged on December 2, 2025 at the Avatar: Fire and Ash premiere. https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/miley-cyrus-maxx-morando-engaged-1235475946/ https://abcnews.com/GMA/Culture/miley-cyrus-engaged-boyfriend-maxx-morando-after-4/story?id=128043079

tweet_summary: Comedian Sammy Obeid posts a clip from his stand-up routine joking about a fictional 'Iranian general' explaining how Charlie Kirk was killed by an explosive in his microphone. The tweet caption is a sarcastic comedy framing, not a sincere factual claim.
why_note_decision: The post is a stand-up comedy routine — Sammy Obeid is a well-known comedian and the bit is openly satirical (e.g. 'like and subscribe to my page'). The audience visibly laughs, the transcript is full of jokes, and the caption is the standard sarcastic-comic framing comics use to promote clips. Notes correcting jokes as if they were earnest claims are false positives. The original note also missed the entire genre and read as humorless pedantry, which is why raters tagged it noteNotNeeded.
judge_guidance: PASS only if the bot declines to write a note. Any note that fact-checks the explosive-microphone / Iranian-general story as if it were a sincere claim — even if factually accurate about Kirk's actual cause of death — is a false positive on a comedy clip. The bot should recognize stand-up satire from the transcript (jokes, audience reaction, comedian's framing) and decline.
original_note_text: This is a stand-up comedy routine, not a factual report. Charlie Kirk was shot and killed at Utah Valley University on September 10, 2025; official FBI and Utah DPS investigations confirm he died from a gunshot wound, not an explosive device. https://dps.utah.gov/press-releases/updates-on-charlie-kirk-shooting-at-uvu/ https://www.fbi.gov/utahvalleyshootingupdates
failure_reason: Note-not-needed: the post is overt comedy/satire; fact-checking the punchline treats a joke as a sincere claim.
importance_lens_rationale: High-engagement post about a politically-charged assassination, but the content is comedy. Suppressing satire with literal fact-checks erodes trust in Community Notes more than it corrects misinformation.

tweet_summary: Ukraine-frontline reporter Caolan (136k followers) posts three images of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth wearing a red-white-and-blue diagonally-striped tie at a White House meeting with Zelensky, plus a screenshot of a 'Russia Plain Flag Tie' product page, alleging Hegseth was signaling Kremlin allegiance. 1.3M impressions, 41k likes.
why_note_decision: The tweet is a political-interpretation claim about color symbolism: 'tie matches Russian flag colors → he's on Kremlin payroll'. The colors red/white/blue are shared by both US and Russian flags, and the diagonal striping is generic (not flag-replica). The original note attempts a factual rebuttal — 'Russian flag has horizontal stripes (white, blue, red)' — which is true but doesn't refute the framing: the tweet doesn't claim the tie is a literal Russian flag, just that the colors signal Russian-aligned sympathy. JD Vance and Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell publicly denied the framing, while Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev embraced it on X — i.e., the dispute is over symbolism/intent, not over geometric fact. Community correctly rejected the note (21 incorrect, 31 opinionSpeculation, 25 missingKeyPoints, 33 noteNotNeeded) — likely because the note's geometric correction doesn't actually engage with the symbolic-signaling claim. A correct bot should decline.
judge_guidance: PASS only if the bot declines to write a note. Any note is a false positive: the tweet makes a political-symbolic interpretation ('Russian-flag colors → Kremlin allegiance'), not a checkable factual assertion. FAIL any note that: (a) repeats the original failure of correcting horizontal-vs-diagonal stripes — the tweet doesn't claim flag-replica geometry, it claims color symbolism, and the colors ARE the same (red/white/blue), (b) cites the marketplace 'Russia Plain Flag Tie' product as if disproving it (the third image shown is exactly this — a real product the tweet acknowledges), (c) editorializes about Hegseth's patriotism or the Vance/Parnell defense, (d) tries to fact-check intent. This is contested political symbolism with both sides publicly framing it (Pentagon: 'patriotic American tie'; Russian envoy Dmitriev: posted with Russian flag emoji) — fact-checking is the wrong move.
original_note_text: The tie worn by Pete Hegseth is not a Russian flag tie. It features diagonal stripes in red, white, and blue—colors shared with the US flag—while the Russian flag has horizontal stripes (white, blue, red). He also wore a US flag pocket square.  https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flag_of_Russia  https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flag_of_the_United_States  https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_flags_with_blue,_red,_and_white_stripes  https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LrIbbS2b2bQ
failure_reason: opinion_speculation — note answers a geometry question the tweet didn't ask. The tweet's claim is about color symbolism/intent, which the note doesn't address. Net effect: defensive partisan framing dressed as fact-check.
importance_lens_rationale: 1.3M impressions, Defense Secretary, Ukraine-war stakes; high prominence but the right call is restraint. Bot must learn that politically-coded color-symbolism claims are opinion, not fact.

tweet_summary: A high-follower partisan account frames Minnesota's voter 'vouching' law as 'voter fraud': says a registered voter can vouch for 8 others with 'No ID required. No proof of residency.' Implies systemic fraud.
why_note_decision: The tweet mixes a true detail (one voter may vouch for up to eight others in their precinct) with a misleading omission ('No ID required'). Under Minn. Stat. 201.061, the person being vouched for STILL must provide their MN driver's license/ID number OR the last four digits of their SSN to verify identity; vouching only substitutes for proof of residency, not for identity verification. Calling this 'voter fraud' on a 2.9M-impression tweet implying a structural exploit warrants a note that supplies the missing identity-verification fact and the historic context (50+ year-old law). The original note merely restated the law without correcting 'No ID required,' which is why raters tagged it noteNotNeeded + missingKeyPoints.
judge_guidance: PASS only if the note (1) confirms vouching is real and lets a registered voter vouch for up to eight others, AND (2) explicitly corrects the tweet's 'No ID required' claim — the registrant must still provide a MN ID/driver's-license number or last 4 of SSN for identity verification; vouching substitutes only for proof of residency. FAIL notes that just restate the law without addressing the 'no ID' misframing. Bonus: note that the law is 50+ years old, and that the voucher signs an oath under penalty of perjury.
reference_note: Minnesota law (Minn. Stat. 201.061) lets a registered precinct voter vouch for up to eight others, but ONLY as proof of residency. The voter still must supply a MN ID/driver's license number or last 4 of SSN for identity verification, and the voucher signs an oath under penalty of perjury. Vouching has existed for 50+ years. https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/201.061 https://www.sos.mn.gov/elections-voting/register-to-vote/register-on-election-day/
original_note_text: Vouching is a legal same-day registration process in Minnesota where a registered precinct voter can vouch for up to eight others per election day by signing an oath attesting to their residency. https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/201.061 https://www.sos.mn.gov/elections-voting/register-to-vote/register-on-election-day/
failure_reason: missing_key_points: restates the law without correcting the tweet's 'No ID required' misframing — the registrant still must provide MN ID/SSN for identity, vouching substitutes only for residency proof
importance_lens_rationale: Election-integrity claims with millions of impressions feed into long-term democratic-discourse trust; correcting the 'no ID required' framing is meaningful for civic infrastructure.

tweet_summary: Clip framed to mock Sen. Fetterman: reporter Manu Raju asks why Congress doesn't 'vote to declare war the way it did with Iraq and Afghanistan'; Fetterman says the last declared war was WWII; Raju says 'No. Iraq and Afghanistan'; Fetterman 'stammers.'
why_note_decision: A note is warranted: the tweet's framing (and the reporter's interjection) wrongly implies Congress formally declared war for Iraq and Afghanistan, making Fetterman appear mistaken. In fact Fetterman is correct - Congress's last formal declaration of war was in 1942 (WWII); Iraq and Afghanistan were authorized via Authorizations for Use of Military Force (AUMFs), which are legally and historically distinct from declarations of war. The note corrects this factual point that many readers got backwards.
judge_guidance: PASS only if the note establishes that Congress did NOT formally declare war for Iraq or Afghanistan - those were AUMFs, legally distinct from declarations of war - and that the last formal US declaration of war was during WWII. It must make clear Fetterman's underlying statement was factually correct (or at minimum that the 'Congress declared war on Iraq/Afghanistan' premise is wrong). FAIL if the note endorses the premise that Iraq/Afghanistan were declared wars, conflates AUMFs with declarations of war, or mocks/sides against Fetterman on the substance. A neutral, sourced explanation of the AUMF-vs-declaration distinction is required.
reference_note: Congress did not declare war in Iraq and Afghanistan, it passed AUMFs which are legally and historically distinct. Scholars have noted that, “Congress issued its last official declaration of war during World War II”     https://education.cfr.org/learn/reading/how-single-phrase-defined-war-terror#:~:text=What%20is%20an%20AUMF?,military%20operations%20since%209/11.
importance_lens_rationale: 1.5M impressions; corrects a widespread civic misconception (AUMF vs declaration of war) on a war-powers question with real governance stakes, and defends an accurate statement against misleading 'gotcha' framing.

tweet_text: American ships crossing the Strait of Hormuz after paying their toll in YUAN - how poetically intoxicating is that?
author_description: Eurasia-wide nomad geopolitical analyst
tweet_summary: Post by geopolitical commentator Pepe Escobar (349k views) claims, as fact, that 'American ships crossing the Strait of Hormuz after paying their toll in YUAN' — framing it as poetic humiliation of the U.S. dollar.
why_note_decision: A note is warranted because the specific claim is false. The toll regime is real: since mid-March 2026 the IRGC has charged ship operators (up to ~$2M/vessel) for Strait of Hormuz passage, payable in yuan or crypto, formalized in the March 30-31 'Strait of Hormuz Management Plan.' BUT Iran's nationality-tiered system DENIES transit entirely to U.S.- and Israel-linked vessels — they are not permitted through, so they are not paying yuan tolls. The image of 'American ships paying tolls in yuan' is unsupported; the U.S. has instead floated its own counter-tolls.
judge_guidance: PASS only if the note corrects the specific false claim — there is no evidence American ships are paying Iranian yuan tolls to cross Hormuz; under Iran's tiered system U.S./Israel-linked vessels are denied passage entirely — while accurately acknowledging the toll regime is real for friendly-nation vessels (yuan/crypto). Source to a credible outlet (Bloomberg / Fortune / Chainalysis / TRM Labs / Time / The Hill). AVOID the original note's failure (rated notHelpfulOpinionSpeculation 5, NoteNotNeeded 5, SourcesMissingOrUnreliable 4, Incorrect 4): the original is essentially correct but reads as partly speculative ('there is no evidence American ships are paying') and leans on Time/Hill links about U.S. counter-tolls; a stronger note explicitly states U.S./Israel vessels are BARRED from transit (so paying is moot) and cites the toll mechanism directly. A note that affirms the tweet (American ships paying yuan tolls) or that denies the toll regime exists at all, fails.
reference_note: No evidence supports American ships paying Iranian tolls in yuan to cross Hormuz. The IRGC toll regime (yuan or crypto, ~$0.50-1/barrel) is real for friendly-nation vessels, but Iran's tiered system bars U.S.- and Israel-linked ships from transit entirely, so they aren't paying these tolls; Washington has floated its own counter-tolls. https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-04-01/strait-of-hormuz-ships-paying-iran-yuan-and-crypto-tolls-for-safe-passage https://fortune.com/2026/04/10/iran-strait-of-hormuz-crypto-tolls-stablecoins-bitcoin-oil-tankers/
original_note_text: While Iran has established a "toll booth" regime requiring payments in yuan or crypto for passage through the Strait of Hormuz, there is no evidence American ships are paying these fees. The U.S. has instead proposed its own counter-tolls on the waterway.  https://time.com/article/2026/04/07/strait-of-hormuz-countries-pass-deals-iran-us-war-trump  https://thehill.com/homenews/administration/5818431-trump-us-tolls-strait-of-hormuz
failure_reason: Substantively correct but rated NOT_HELPFUL (15 ratings; dominant notHelpfulOpinionSpeculation 5, NoteNotNeeded 5, SourcesMissingOrUnreliable 4, Incorrect 4). The 'there is no evidence American ships are paying' phrasing proves a negative and reads as speculative; it misses the cleaner, stronger fact that U.S./Israel-linked vessels are categorically BARRED from transit under Iran's tiered system, so the premise of 'American ships paying' is moot. Sources are about U.S. counter-tolls rather than the bar on U.S. vessels.
importance_lens_rationale: 349k impressions amplifying a 'dollar humiliated' narrative during wartime; correcting the false 'American ships paying yuan' specifics matters for accurate public understanding of the conflict's economic dimension and de-dollarization claims.

tweet_summary: User 'steve' (114k followers, retired retailer) posts an image of a textured steering wheel with overlay text 'Just realised that these little bumps on the steering wheel are in Braille so that blind drivers have no trouble finding the horn'. 683k impressions, 5.9k likes, 547 RTs. Caption: 'I never knew this !!! Everyday is a school day'.
why_note_decision: This is a well-documented viral hoax that resurfaces periodically. Reuters, USA Today, and Snopes have all debunked it: the bumps are tactile/grip texture (or markers for assembly orientation), not Braille; blind individuals are not legally permitted to drive. Author tweets it sincerely ('I never knew this'); most replies treat it as truth or as a joke about blind drivers. With 683k impressions and the author expressly endorsing the false fact, a note IS warranted. The original note's substance is correct; rating likely fell to NoteNotNeeded (7/13) because many readers see the obvious joke premise (blind drivers) and dismiss the underlying false-fact claim as harmless.
judge_guidance: PASS only if the note (a) states the bumps are NOT Braille (typically tactile grip/texture or assembly markers), (b) notes that blind people are not legally permitted to drive, and (c) cites Reuters, USA Today, or Snopes fact-checks. AVOID over-explaining or moralizing. A note that merely calls it a joke without addressing the false-fact claim fails because the author tweets it sincerely. FAIL any note that endorses the Braille claim.
reference_note: The raised bumps on car steering wheels are not Braille — they are tactile grip texture (and on some models, alignment markers from assembly). Blind people are not legally permitted to drive in the US, UK, or other jurisdictions. The 'Braille horn' claim is a long-running viral hoax debunked by Reuters, USA Today, and Snopes. https://www.reuters.com/article/world/fact-check-bumps-on-car-steering-wheel-are-not-in-braille-idUSKBN25V1US https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/factcheck/2020/09/24/fact-check-raised-dots-steering-wheel-not-braille/5839064002
original_note_text: The raised bumps on steering wheels are not Braille for blind drivers but tactile markers to help all drivers locate the horn; blind individuals are not legally permitted to drive. https://www.reuters.com/article/world/fact-check-bumps-on-car-steering-wheel-are-not-in-braille-idUSKBN25V1US https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/braille-in-some-steering-wheels https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/factcheck/2020/09/24/fact-check-raised-dots-steering-wheel-not-braille/5839064002
failure_reason: Substantively correct but rated notHelpfulNoteNotNeeded (7/13) plus MissingKeyPoints (5). Likely because many readers treat the post as obvious humor about blind drivers and dismiss the false-fact below it. Could read more crisply.
importance_lens_rationale: 683k impressions on a sincere endorsement of a well-known false fact; low stakes individually but characteristic of viral false-fact creep — useful baseline for note-warranted-but-rated-not-needed pattern.

tweet_summary: Viral post (838k views, 38k likes, by 'Basil the Great', 311k followers) headline-screams 'LEAKED EMAIL REVEALS KING CHARLES AIDE OVERSAW ROYAL PROTECTION AT EPSTEIN ISLAND'. The DOJ-released emails actually concern Met protection officers staying at Epstein's Manhattan townhouse on East 71st Street during Prince Andrew's November–December 2010 US trip, NOT Little St. James ('Epstein Island').
why_note_decision: A note IS warranted. 'Epstein Island' (Little St. James, USVI) is a culturally loaded location synonymous with the trafficking allegations. Conflating it with Epstein's Manhattan townhouse materially changes the implication of the story (from 'royal aide arranged stays at island where trafficking allegedly occurred' to 'royal aide arranged officer lodging at NYC townhouse during an official visit'). The underlying GB News reporting is real (Peter Loughborough, then-commander of Met royalty protection, allegedly oversaw the arrangement; Officer Julian Phillips arrived Nov 28, 2010 at the £43M 7th-floor 71st Street townhouse). The headline-level location swap is a checkable factual error that 838k viewers benefit from being corrected on. Provisional 'no_note_needed' label is wrong.
judge_guidance: PASS only if the note (a) corrects the location: the DOJ-released emails describe Met protection officers staying at Epstein's Manhattan townhouse (East 71st Street, NYC) during Prince Andrew's 2010 US trip — NOT Little St. James ('Epstein Island'); and (b) cites a credible primary report (GB News, AOL, ABC News, or the original DOJ files) — not low-tier conspiracy aggregators (amg-news, davidicke). A note that simply says 'no evidence' without naming the correct location FAILS (the story is real, only the location is wrong). A note that defends the King or denies Loughborough's role categorically FAILS too — palace sources only said the deployment 'wouldn't have required his direct approval', not that the underlying email exchange is fabricated. AVOID the original note's failure: it correctly distinguishes townhouse vs. island but raters tagged it MissingKeyPoints (4) — likely because it underplays that the story itself (officers staying at the townhouse, arranged via Andrew's secretary to Epstein's executive assistant) is confirmed and serious. A correct note should both fix the location AND acknowledge officers did stay at Epstein's NYC townhouse.
reference_note: Misleading framing: the leaked DOJ emails describe Met protection officers staying at Epstein's Manhattan townhouse (East 71st Street, NYC) for ~9 days during Prince Andrew's 2010 US trip, not at Little St. James ('Epstein Island'). The arrangement was reportedly coordinated between Andrew's then-secretary Amanda Thirsk and Epstein's assistant Lesley Groff; Peter Loughborough then commanded Scotland Yard's royalty/diplomatic protection unit. A Palace source said the specific deployment wouldn't have required his direct approval. https://www.gbnews.com/royal/king-charles-peter-loughborough-epstein-files https://abcnews.com/US/fallout-epstein-files-release-reaches-highest-levels-uk/story?id=129893095
original_note_text: Misleading: GB News reports DOJ emails show Peter Loughborough arranged Met officers to stay at Epstein's Manhattan townhouse during a 2010 official trip, not on Little St James ('Epstein Island'). A Palace source says no direct approval was required. https://www.gbnews.com/royal/king-charles-peter-loughborough-epstein-files https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_N._Straus_House
failure_reason: Note has the right correction (townhouse vs island) but raters flagged MissingKeyPoints (4), IrrelevantSources (2, the Wikipedia townhouse-architecture link is tangential), and OpinionSpeculation (2). Likely under-emphasizes that the underlying story — officers did sleep at Epstein's NYC townhouse for ~9 days, arranged via Andrew's secretary — IS confirmed, while spending words on the palace-source exoneration ('no direct approval was required') which reads as defensive framing. Net result: rated NEEDS_MORE_RATINGS, no clear push to HELPFUL.
importance_lens_rationale: 838k impressions on a high-profile UK royal/Epstein story; 'Epstein Island' is a politically and emotionally loaded location. From an info-integrity lens, conflating the NYC townhouse with Little St. James inflates the implication into trafficking-site association and is exactly the class of subtle location swap that benefits from a precise correction.

tweet_summary: Sen. Scott Wiener quotes/characterizes Trump's real Thanksgiving 2025 Truth Social post (the screenshot in the tweet is the genuine post), framing it as Trump declaring '53M non-citizens criminals' and announcing denaturalization, 'reverse migration' and 'whites-only immigration'.
why_note_decision: The underlying screenshot is Trump's authentic Thanksgiving 2025 post, which really does cite a 53M foreign-born figure, calls most of them welfare/prison/gang/cartel cases, and announces a permanent migration pause, denaturalization, and 'REVERSE MIGRATION'. Wiener's tweet is an op-ed characterization of that real post ('declares 53M criminals', 'whites-only immigration', 'Reichstag Fire'). These are contested political interpretations of genuinely-made statements, not checkable factual fabrications. The original note tried to 'debunk' the 53M figure as if the tweet author invented it, but the figure is Trump's own and the policies described are real. A note here injects a contested counter-framing onto accurate reporting of a public official's words.
judge_guidance: PASS only if the bot declines to write a note. The tweet accurately reflects a real Trump Truth Social post (shown in the image): the 53M foreign-population figure, mass-deportation/denaturalization/'reverse migration' plans are all genuinely his. The author's gloss ('whites-only', 'Reichstag Fire', 'declares them all criminals') is political opinion about a real document, not a fabricated fact. Any note that (a) treats the 53M figure as the author's own invention to be debunked, or (b) 'corrects' Wiener's characterization of real Trump statements, is a false positive. The original note's specific failure was citing a 2024 FactCheck.org article about a different Trump chart and implying the tweet fabricated the claim — a correct response must avoid that and recognize the post is contested opinion on accurate reporting.
original_note_text: Misleading: Trump's "53M" mixes legal and unauthorized foreign-born and wrongly implies they're all criminals; FactCheck has debunked similar claims. Media report his migration pause and denaturalization plans, but denaturalization is reported as targeted, not a blanket purge. https://www.factcheck.org/2024/04/trumps-misleading-chart-on-illegal-immigration/
failure_reason: Note treats the tweet as if it fabricated the 53M claim and 'corrects' the author, but the figure and policies are Trump's own real Thanksgiving post; cites an unrelated 2024 FactCheck article. Rated notHelpfulIncorrect / NoteNotNeeded — it argues against an accurate characterization of a public official's statements (opinion target).
importance_lens_rationale: High-stakes immigration/denaturalization rhetoric from a sitting president affects rule-of-law norms, but the tweet is a senator's accurate (if charged) summary; little misinformation to correct, so corrective value is low.

why_note_decision: The tweet's central claim — that the account is a staged/fake 'PR bot' profile — is false. Sharma genuinely shared her real gamertag (AMRAHSAHSA); the account shows authentic, varied gaming activity over a month (multiple games, real playtimes), and she publicly explained the inflated gamerscore as her family having shared the account, which she then restricted to herself. The 'all same date' premise is wrong. The post drives a xenophobic harassment pile-on in replies, so a corrective note is warranted.
judge_guidance: PASS only if the note establishes that the account is authentic (Sharma's real, publicly shared gamertag) and rebuts the 'fake PR bot' / 'all achievements same date' premise with the key fact the original note OMITTED: the elevated gamerscore came from family members sharing the account, which Sharma herself publicly acknowledged and then limited to just herself. A passing note should also note the activity is spread across many games/dates with real playtimes. It must NOT merely quibble over 'Jan 15 not 16' without addressing the substance, and must NOT concede the PR-bot framing. Cite a credible gaming outlet (Windows Central, Pure Xbox, TrueAchievements).
reference_note: This is Asha Sharma's real Xbox gamertag, which she shared publicly; it is not a fabricated 'PR bot' account. The achievements span many games over weeks with genuine playtimes (e.g., narrative titles played at length), not a single pre-set date. Sharma explained the high gamerscore was because her family had been sharing the account, which she has since limited to herself. https://www.windowscentral.com/gaming/xbox/newly-named-xbox-ceo-asha-sharma-has-shared-her-gamertag-so-what-is-she-playing-and-why-does-it-matter
original_note_text: Sharma's first achievement was Jan 15 (not 16), with varied dates & playtimes (13+ hrs in Halo, 100% Firewatch completed Jan 20). failure_reason: Missing key points: leads with a pedantic 'Jan 15 not 16' correction and isolated playtime stats but omits the single most decisive, publicly-documented rebuttal — that Sharma explained the apparent anomalies as her family sharing the account. Reads as an unsourced-feeling spot-check rather than the clear authenticity explanation a reader needs.
importance_lens_rationale: 1.6M impressions and an explicitly xenophobic harassment campaign ('their degrees are fake too,' 'thanks India') against a named executive; correcting fabricated inauthenticity accusations reduces real harassment harm.

FAIL if the note treats the citizenship/passport claim as plausibly true or cites the satire page as a credible source. Sources must be reliable (a fact-check or the satire page's own disclaimer), not the viral image.

tweet_summary: Elon Musk: '800k voters found to be improperly registered to vote in Oregon' — quoting a post about Oregon planning to remove up to 800,000 inactive voters from registration rolls.
why_note_decision: Note is warranted. The framing 'improperly registered to vote' implies these are ineligible/fraudulent registrations — but they are simply long-inactive voter records (people who moved, died, or stopped voting). Oregon SoS Tobias Read agreed to the removal under a Judicial Watch lawsuit settlement; Oregon will cancel registrations that already met legal removal criteria before 2017 (returned mail, failed to respond to notices, missed multiple federal elections). These voters did NOT receive ballots and had NO effect on elections. The actual count is 'up to 800,000', not a confirmed 800K. The original AI note covers this correctly ('routine cleanup prompted by lawsuits; outdated records of real people who haven't voted recently, not fake or fraudulent entries') — but somehow got 527 'note not needed' votes vs 461 'missing key points'. The tweet IS misleading because 'improperly registered' carries fraud connotations that the underlying story doesn't support; a note is warranted. The original note is actually pretty good and may have been a victim of partisan downvoting.
judge_guidance: PASS if the note establishes: (1) Oregon is removing up to ~800,000 INACTIVE voter records (not 'improperly registered' in the sense of fraud); (2) these are real people who haven't voted in years / moved / had mail returned; (3) inactive voters do NOT receive ballots and had no effect on elections; (4) the cleanup is the result of a settlement with Judicial Watch under federal voter-roll-maintenance law. reference_note: Oregon is removing up to ~800,000 inactive voter records under a settlement with Judicial Watch — these are long-inactive registrations (people who moved, missed multiple federal elections, or had mail returned), not fraudulent entries. Despite the bio's blanket 'satire' label, the clip has 1.43M views and is widely shared and consumed credulously (replies treat it as proof the leaders are 'puppets'), and it is a repeatedly-debunked deepfake of world leaders. A note is warranted; the blanket bio disclaimer does not neutralize a viral false-provenance claim.
judge_guidance: PASS only if the note (a) states the video is digitally manipulated / deepfaked — NOT authentic footage of Macron or Zelensky dancing — with Macron's face superimposed onto unrelated archival dancers, AND (b) is clearly worded and easy to parse. It must AVOID the original note's failure of being hard to understand: do NOT bury the point in a confusing clause like 'most originating from his pre-presidency comedy sketches'. It is fine to briefly note Zelensky was a pre-presidency entertainer, but the core message — the footage is fake/manipulated — must be unambiguous. Cite a reputable fact-check. FAIL if the note treats the dancing footage as real, or is so convoluted a reader cannot tell what is being corrected.

tweet_summary: A 'Curiosity' science-content account posts a video of a sweeping panoramic Martian landscape, calling it real footage from Mars from 140M miles away. The video shows the rover's robotic arm coming into frame and matches the look of NASA's recent Perseverance/Curiosity panoramas.
why_note_decision: The original note flatly claims 'this video is not authentic Mars rover footage; smooth panning videos like this are simulations or stitched panoramas'. This is wrong on its face: NASA released exactly this type of high-resolution, smooth-panning 360-degree panorama from both Curiosity (1.5-billion-pixel mosaic of 1,031 images, Nov-Dec 2025) and Perseverance (980-image panorama, Dec 2025-Jan 2026), and the rover-arm-coming-into-frame matches a real Perseverance/Curiosity composition. The 'stitched panorama' framing in the note ISN'T disqualifying — NASA's official panoramas ARE stitched panoramas, and that's how rover panoramic video has always been built; the rover doesn't have a high-frame-rate movie camera. The note also cites a Forbes 2021 piece and a Mashable piece about a different fake video from 2021 plus a Snopes Mars-audio fact-check — none of which establish the video here is fake. The tweet itself doesn't claim it's a continuous live shot. So a CN denying authenticity is itself misinformation — a clear false-positive case.
judge_guidance: PASS only if the bot declines to write a note. NASA released ultra-high-resolution stitched panoramas from Curiosity (Nov-Dec 2025, 1.5 gigapixel) and Perseverance (Dec 2025-Jan 2026) that are exactly this kind of footage. The original note's claim that 'smooth panning videos like this are simulations' is itself misinformation — NASA panoramic 'videos' are routinely composed from many still images, and that doesn't make them fake. Specifically FAIL any note that (a) says the video is AI-generated, a simulation, or not real Mars footage, (b) cites the Snopes 'Mars audio' fact-check or the 2021 Forbes/Mashable pieces about an unrelated viral fake video as if they cover this one, or (c) characterizes 'stitched panorama' as disqualifying. A note would only be warranted if the bot can identify a specific provenance issue (e.g. the clip is actually a CGI render from a particular game/film, or the rover-arm in this composition does not correspond to any released NASA panorama).
original_note_text: This video is not authentic Mars rover footage; smooth panning videos like this are simulations or stitched panoramas, while real rover media uses still images or low-frame-rate clips. https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/mars-real-audio https://mashable.com/article/mars-perseverance-fake-video https://www.forbes.com/sites/ericmack/2021/02/21/the-mars-rover-viral-video-going-around-isnt-what-it-seems
failure_reason: incorrect_note — denies authenticity of footage that matches NASA's recently released Perseverance/Curiosity panoramas; conflates 'stitched panorama' with 'not real Mars footage'. Sources cited are about a different 2021 viral fake video and Mars audio, not this clip.
importance_lens_rationale: Science-popularization content; bad notes that 'debunk' real NASA footage degrade public trust in real science — small absolute harm but emblematic of false-positive risks.

why_note_decision: Several figures are substantially overstated and the methodology is misleading. Brazil's 112.7M (#1) counts all 'pardo' (mixed-race) Brazilians as 'African' — the 2022 census recorded ~20.7M Black (preto) plus ~92.1M pardo, so labeling ~112M as 'Africans' conflates mixed-race with Black/African. France's figure is ~3.8-6M (not 10M; France doesn't officially track race), Colombia's Afro-descendant population is ~4.9M (not 15M), and the UK's is ~2.4-2.5M (not 4.9M). A note clarifying the inflation/methodology is warranted.
judge_guidance: PASS only if the note flags that the figures are overstated and/or the methodology is misleading. Strongest points to make: Brazil's 112.7M conflates mixed-race ('pardo', ~92M) with Black/African (~20.7M Black per the 2022 census), so it overstates the 'African' count; Colombia's Afro-descendant population is ~4.9M (not 15M); France's is ~3.8-6M and not officially counted by race (not 10M); the UK's is ~2.4-2.5M (not 4.9M). A correct note should at minimum challenge the inflated figures (ideally including the Brazil conflation, the single biggest distortion) rather than only nitpicking one country. FAIL a note that endorses the chart's totals as accurate.

Colombia's Afro-descendant population is ~4.9M (not 15M), France's is ~3.8-6M (race isn't officially counted; not 10M), and the UK's is ~2.4-2.5M (not 4.9M). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afro-Brazilians https://worldpopulationreview.com/country-rankings/african-diaspora-countries

tweet_summary: Nick Fuentes asserts that for decades Israel has 'openly pursued an agenda to topple Iraq, Syria, and Iran' and 'orchestrated all of these wars' to gain 'total hegemony over the Middle East' — framed as the real reason for the ongoing US-Iran conflict.
why_note_decision: This is a sweeping antisemitic-conspiracy-coded historical claim that misrepresents a real policy document. The 1996 'A Clean Break' memo (authored by Perle/Feith/Wurmser et al. for Netanyahu) does propose weakening regional rivals — that part is real and citeable. But the tweet's claim that Israel 'orchestrated' the Iraq War, the Syria conflict, and the current Iran war is not supported by mainstream historiography: those conflicts had US/regional drivers. The claim is widely promoted in white-nationalist/'Groypers' spaces and converted into 'Greater Israel' rhetoric. With 5.2M impressions and replies amplifying overt antisemitism, a note is warranted. The original note was rated NOT_HELPFUL primarily because raters disagreed politically (high notHelpfulOpinionSpeculation/Argumentative tags) — that doesn't mean a note isn't needed; it means the bar is high.
judge_guidance: A correct note must (1) NOT endorse the conspiracy framing, (2) acknowledge that 'A Clean Break' (1996) is a real document advocating weakening Iraq/Syria/Iran, (3) state that mainstream historians/declassified records attribute the Iraq War, Syrian civil war, and US-Iran conflict primarily to US, regional, and domestic Iraqi/Syrian/Iranian drivers — not to Israeli orchestration, (4) cite at least one neutral mainstream source (e.g. Wikipedia on the Iraq War, CFR/RAND, or major newspapers). MUST NOT repeat the original note's specific failures: do not editorialize ('disputed/debunked'), do not stack ideologically slanted opinion sites as primary sources, keep tone neutral. PASS if the note clearly contests the 'orchestrated all these wars' claim with neutral sources and stays under 280 chars; FAIL if it (a) is argumentative/biased, (b) cites only opinion/advocacy sites, or (c) accepts the conspiracy framing.
reference_note: Israel's 1996 'A Clean Break' memo did urge weakening regional rivals (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Clean_Break:_A_New_Strategy_for_Securing_the_Realm), but mainstream historians attribute the Iraq War, Syrian civil war, and US–Iran conflict mainly to US decision-making and regional/local drivers — not Israeli orchestration. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq_War

tweet_summary: A pro-Ukraine OSINT account posts video of Russian soldiers training with green pop-up tents, hedging that this is 'some unknown technology... apparently' an individual tent for infantry to wear during assaults / winter.
why_note_decision: The tweet is substantially accurate and appropriately hedged ('unknown technology', 'apparently'). Russian forces ARE documented repurposing commercial portable shower/toilet tents as individual concealment shelters against FPV/thermal drones (Militarnyi, United24, The Sun); the video's own audio is a Russian instructor training troops to wear, fold and walk in the tents — i.e. they are genuinely being fielded as individual infantry shelters. The original note's framing ('these are commercial pop-up privacy shelters... NOT new military technology for infantry protection during assaults') is the misleading part: it is true they are commercial tents, but false to imply they are not being used militarily — Russia is in fact deploying them as improvised infantry concealment. The note injects a dismissive counter-narrative against accurate reporting, so no note is needed.
judge_guidance: PASS only if the bot declines to write a corrective note. The tweet correctly (and hedged) reports a REAL, OSINT-documented Russian tactic: commercial pop-up shower/toilet tents repurposed as individual soldier shelters to evade FPV/thermal drones. CRITICAL FAIL: any note that, like the original, claims these are 'just commercial privacy/toilet tents, NOT military technology / not for infantry protection' — that contradicts documented reporting and the video's own training audio. A purely additive note noting the tents are repurposed civilian products AND that Russia is using them for drone concealment would be borderline-acceptable context, but a note framed as a debunk of the tweet should FAIL.
original_note_text: The tents depicted are commercial pop-up privacy shelters for use as changing rooms or portable toilets, not new military technology for infantry protection during assaults. https://www.ebay.com/p/Army-Green-Portable-Changing-Room-Shower-Tent-Camp-Toilet-Pop-up-Privacy-Shelter/501262754 https://tuffstuffoverland.com/products/tuff-stuff-r-portable-outdoor-toilet-tent
failure_reason: Half-true but misleadingly dismissive: correct that the tents are commercial products, but wrong to imply they are not being used militarily. Russia is documented repurposing them as individual infantry concealment vs drones; the tweet's hedged report is accurate. Sources are shopping listings, not reporting on the tactic.
importance_lens_rationale: Ukraine-war OSINT with ~667k views; accurate battlefield-adaptation reporting. Mild progress/discourse value in not letting a dismissive false 'correction' bury a real story; not high-stakes misinfo.

The note must AVOID the original's failure of relying solely on a hard-to-verify Persian URL + an Instagram reel; it should cite a clearer source or at minimum present the provenance plainly (Iranian news coverage of the teacher Rahim Nasrallahi grieving his student Aydın). FAIL if it endorses the war-casualty framing, claims the video is fake/AI (it is real), or offers no provenance.
